lead:
Panchakarma, Sanskrit for 'five actions', is the best-known cleansing programme in Ayurveda, India's traditional medicine system. It combines oil massage, steam, herbal therapies and purification procedures meant to remove accumulated 'toxins' and rebalance the body's doshas.
People seeking better skin, energy and a rested look sometimes book it as a retreat or clinic course. Research is mostly small pilot studies, case reports and metabolomic work on general health measures; no trial has tested appearance outcomes directly.

paras: Programmes are usually run at Ayurvedic clinics or retreats over days to weeks under a practitioner. They commonly begin with preparatory oil treatment and sweating, move to the purification therapies chosen for the individual, and end with a recovery diet and herbal regimen. Stated goals include clearer skin, hair and general vitality.

Purgative, emetic and enema-based therapies can cause dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and other adverse effects, particularly in people with medical conditions. Wikipedia notes that many Ayurvedic preparations, particularly in the rasashastra tradition, contain lead, mercury and arsenic. Practitioners and clinical guidelines emphasise individual assessment and supervision.

angle.text: Practitioners present Panchakarma as a way to cleanse the body and rebalance the doshas, with better skin and vitality as expected side benefits. People book it as a retreat or clinic course for a refreshed look.

lead: Panchakarma is a purification regimen in Ayurveda, the traditional medicine system of India. The name refers to five main procedures, taught as a way to expel accumulated waste (ama) and restore balance among the three doshas, vata, pitta and kapha.[1][2]

For appearance, it is sought by people who associate internal cleansing with clearer skin, a brighter complexion and less visible fatigue, and it is a common offering at wellness retreats. Ayurvedic texts and practitioners present it as constitutional treatment tailored to the individual rather than a cosmetic procedure.[2][3]

Published research includes a metabolomic study of a Panchakarma-based programme in healthy people, small clinical studies of the therapy in specific conditions, and historical and safety-oriented reviews. No measurements of skin or other appearance outcomes have been reported.
infobox: Clinic or retreat programme, days to weeks
Varies by country; Ayurvedic practice is regulated mainly in India

paras: Ayurveda holds that health depends on balance among the doshas and that blocked channels (srotas) can be opened by oil massage and fomentation.[1] Panchakarma is the cleansing branch of this system, delivered after preparatory therapies and followed by a rebuilding diet.[2]
Treatments are individualised by practitioner assessment of a person's constitution (prakruti) and condition.[4]

Panchakarma comes from classical Ayurvedic texts. A 2024 review credits Tryambak Mahadev Gogate (1913-1998) with developing practical applications of the therapies during the colonial period, partly through self-experimentation.[5] Interest outside India has grown through wellness tourism and integrative-medicine centres, including Maharishi Ayurveda clinics.[6]

A 2016 study of a Panchakarma-based intervention in healthy participants reported changes in metabolomic profiles.[7] A 2009 paper discussed measuring the effects of Ayurveda and Panchakarma as a holistic intervention.[8]

A pilot study at the Maharishi Ayurveda Health Centre in Norway followed women with fibromyalgia for 24 months after a treatment programme.[6] A randomised open-label study tested a Panchakarma-based add-on therapy alongside standard care in chronic heart failure.[9] Single-case reports describe Panchakarma in conditions such as chronic urticaria and autoimmune pancreatitis.[10][11] No study has measured skin appearance or other cosmetic outcomes as the main result.

Wikipedia's Ayurveda article reports that many preparations, particularly in the rasashastra tradition, contain toxic levels of lead, mercury and arsenic, and describes the theory and practice of Ayurveda as pseudoscientific.[1] Practitioners counter that Panchakarma is supervised, individualised therapy. Guidelines for safer Panchakarma practice were published in the Journal of Ayurveda and Integrative Medicine in 2022.[12]
